lesson.title: The Shape You Can Actually See
lesson.summary: Molecular geometry describes the three dimensional arrangement of a molecule's atoms alone, ignoring the invisible lone pairs, and it is this visible shape that chemists use to predict polarity, reactivity, and physical behavior.
lesson.body:
Electron geometry describes every electron domain around a central atom, bonding pairs and lone pairs alike. Molecular geometry narrows that picture down to only what you could actually point to with a model kit: the positions of the atoms. Lone pairs still exist, they still occupy space, and they still exert repulsion exactly as VSEPR predicts, but they are left out of the name given to the shape because there is no atom there to trace an outline around. This distinction, invisible influence versus visible outline, is the single most important idea to hold onto when moving from electron geometry to molecular geometry.

When a central atom has no lone pairs at all, electron geometry and molecular geometry are identical, since every domain is a bonding pair connected to a visible atom. The moment lone pairs enter the picture, the two names diverge, even though the underlying electron arrangement has not changed. Ammonia, NH3, is the clearest way to see this. Its electron geometry is tetrahedral, four domains, three bonding pairs and one lone pair, spread out 109.5 degrees apart in principle. But molecular geometry only names the positions of the four atoms, nitrogen and three hydrogens, and once the lone pair is left out of the naming, that shape is called trigonal pyramidal, like a tripod with nitrogen at the peak.

Crucially, removing the lone pair from the name does not remove it from the physics. The lone pair on nitrogen is still there, still repelling the three N to H bonding pairs, and that repulsion is exactly why the measured H to N to H bond angle in ammonia is about 107 degrees rather than the ideal tetrahedral value of 109.5 degrees. Molecular geometry describes what a chemist can see and measure between atoms, but the invisible lone pair is doing real work behind the scenes, compressing the visible angles closer together than a perfectly symmetric tetrahedral arrangement would allow.

Molecular geometry matters far beyond naming conventions because it directly controls measurable properties like polarity. A molecule with individually polar bonds is not automatically a polar molecule overall, the shape decides whether those bond dipoles cancel out or add up. Water is the classic demonstration: each O to H bond is polar, but if water were linear the two bond dipoles would point in opposite directions and cancel completely, leaving a nonpolar molecule. Because water's molecular geometry is bent rather than linear, the two O to H dipoles do not cancel, and the molecule ends up strongly polar, which is central to why water dissolves so many other substances and forms hydrogen bonds with itself.

The general procedure for finding molecular geometry always follows the same four steps: draw a correct Lewis structure, count the total electron domains on the central atom to find the electron geometry, identify how many of those domains are lone pairs rather than bonding pairs, and then apply the appropriate molecular geometry name for that specific combination. The chapters that follow work through each of these named shapes in turn, linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, octahedral, bent, and trigonal pyramidal, each one a direct consequence of a particular steric number paired with a particular number of lone pairs.
